title: Optimization of a hyperspectral imaging system for rapid detection of microplastics down to 100 µm
author: Zhu, Kanaya, et al.
materials: One of the traditional methods to identify microplastic particles is direct visual observation using optical microscopy [8] where erroneous recognition and miscounting could occur [12]. Other common methods use Fourier transform infrared and Raman spectroscopy [13,18], and these spectroscopic methods are more advantageous than optical microscopy for accurate quantification of both plastic numbers and polymer types [17]. Fries et al. [6] used pyrolysis-gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry and scanning electron microscopy to identify plastic polymers and associated additives. Furthermore, Nile Red staining and subsequent detection of fluorescence has been applied to rapidly detect microplastics, but spectroscopic techniques are still needed for polymer type classification [11]. With all of these methods, pretreatments are needed, and these are time-consuming and laborious [16]. Therefore, methods for rapid and convenient quantification of environmental microplastic particles are crucial.

steps.title: Assemble default imaging system
steps.instruction: Mount the Pika NIR-640 hyperspectral camera on a tower, attach a 25 mm focal‑length lens (pixel size 15 µm), install the four halogen lamps on the tower between camera and translation stage, connect the translation stage to the system, link the computer to both camera and stage, and launch Spectronon Pro software.

substeps.instruction: Connect computer to camera and stage.

steps.title: Calibrate reflectance mode
steps.instruction: Measure dark current with the objective lens blocked and subtract it from all data, then scale the signal to absolute reflectance (reflectance = 1) using a gold‑coated polycarbonate filter (GPC0847‑BA, Structure Probe, Inc., USA). After focusing the lens, adjust scanning speed and frame rate to obtain a near‑true aspect ratio.

substeps.instruction: Block objective lens and record dark current.
Subtract dark current from all subsequent data.
Place gold‑coated polycarbonate filter (GPC0847‑BA) and record reflectance = 1.
Adjust focus of the objective lens.
Tune scanning speed and frame rate for near‑true aspect ratio.

steps.title: Set default imaging parameters
steps.instruction: Position the camera ~33 cm from the translation stage (camera‑to‑lamps = 13 cm, lamps‑to‑stage = 20 cm) to avoid heating, then set scanning speed to 1.5876 cm s⁻¹, frame rate to 100 Hz, integration time to 7.814 ms, and acquire a scan of 600 lines; under these conditions the minimal detectable microplastic size is ~250 µm.

substeps.instruction: Set camera‑to‑stage distance ≈ 33 cm (camera‑to‑lamps 13 cm, lamps‑to‑stage 20 cm).

steps.title: Replace lamps with NIR sources
steps.instruction: Remove the four halogen lamps and install two converged‑light NIR lamps (LN‑200CIR, CCS Inc., Japan) covering 400–2500 nm on the left and right sides of the system to reduce radiant heat. Verify illumination by imaging 300 µm polyethylene particles and confirm a stable baseline of 0.95–0.99 (1000–1600 nm) and better feature visibility at 1540–1550 nm compared with the original lamps.

substeps.instruction: Mount two NIR lamps (LN‑200CIR) symmetrically left and right.
Confirm lamps cover 400–2500 nm and emit low heat.
Record baseline reflectance (0.95–0.99, 1000–1600 nm) and feature at 1540–1550 nm.

steps.title: Install extension tube for macro
steps.instruction: Insert a Thorlabs CMV10 extension tube between the lens and camera, lower the camera to reduce the lens‑to‑subject distance, and place the camera‑lens assembly ≈ 3 cm above the translation stage to achieve macro‑photography magnification.

substeps.instruction: Insert CMV10 extension tube between lens and camera.
Lower camera to decrease focusing distance.
Position camera‑lens assembly ~3 cm above stage.

steps.title: Adjust exposure and aspect ratio
steps.instruction: Because macro‑photography reduces per‑pixel exposure, retune scanning speed to 0.07938 cm s⁻¹, keep frame rate at 100 Hz and integration time at 7.814 ms; acquire a 600‑line scan in ~7 s, resulting in a pixel size of 14.8 µm and a near‑true aspect ratio.

steps.title: Validate detection with default system
steps.instruction: Place PE particles of 2000 µm, 1000 µm, 500 µm, and 300 µm on the gold‑coated filter and image with the default parameters; record pixel counts (36, 16, 4, and 1 respectively) and note high noise and dampened features for 300 µm. Classify using Spectral Angle Mapper with a pre‑acquired PE reference spectrum, concluding reliable detection only for particles >500 µm.

substeps.instruction: Deposit PE particles (2000, 1000, 500, 300 µm) on filter.
Apply Spectral Angle Mapper using reference PE spectrum.

steps.title: Validate detection with modified system
steps.instruction: Using the modified setup, image PE particles ranging from 1000 µm down to 100 µm; observe distinct spectral features at 1150–1250 nm and 1350–1450 nm even for 100 µm particles, and classify them successfully with SAM, confirming detection down to 100 µm and capability to identify 11 common polymer types.

substeps.instruction: Place PE particles (1000–100 µm) on filter.
Verify spectral features at 1150–1250 nm and 1350–1450 nm for all sizes.
Confirm detection of particles as small as 100 µm.
Note system can detect 11 polymer types.
